title: Layered architecture
idea: Layered architecture splits a system into frontend, API, service, domain and database. Each layer has one job, and calls point inward, never outward.

analogy.text: A theatre: the box office deals with the audience, the director decides what happens, and stagehands move props. The box office never walks onto the stage.
analogy.breaks: Here each layer can be swapped for a fake in a test.

points: The controller turns HTTP into a method call and back; it holds no rules.
The service runs one use case, usually inside one transaction.
Domain classes hold state and invariants and know nothing of HTTP or SQL.
The repository is an interface: memory in tests, PostgreSQL in production.

steps.caption: The frontend sends a slot and a patient. It never talks to the database.
The controller checks the body's shape. Bad input stops here with 400.
The service runs the booking use case and opens one transaction.
The domain model applies its own rules, such as which status changes are legal.
The service passes the checked object to the repository, which writes the row. Constraints are the last guard.
The service gets a domain object back, never raw SQL rows.
The controller maps the result to 201 and a JSON body.
If the slot was taken, the service throws instead, and the controller maps that to 409.

code.title: Four layers in Java
code.caption: The layers in one file so you can see the boundaries. This book models the domain in Java; the Express chapters hold the same rules in JavaScript.

walk.text: Wire the layers by hand: repository into service, service into controller.
The controller rejects bad input and maps outcomes to status codes.
The service applies the rule: one live appointment per slot.
The domain record guards its fields and knows how a booking starts.
The service depends on this interface, not on any database.
An in-memory repository for the demo; a PostgreSQL one has the same methods.

pitfalls: Do not put SQL in controllers; one route then mixes three layers' jobs.
Do not return database rows to clients; map them to an API shape.
Check-then-save in the service still races; page 5 adds locks and constraints.

quiz.q: What does the second line of Layers print?
quiz.why: SL-1 already has a BOOKED appointment, so `findLiveBySlot` finds it. The service throws and the controller maps the exception to 409.

takeaway: Each layer has one job, and calls point inward, never outward.

starters: Where does validation belong: controller, service or domain?
Should the service return domain objects or DTOs?
Is a repository interface worth it if I only ever use PostgreSQL?
